note: Real port cities of the ~1500-1650 Age of Sail. lat/lon are Wikidata property P625 (CC0), fetched by scripts/fetch-coords.mjs and never hand-typed; `source` records the exact item each coordinate came from. `sea`, `region`, `tier`, `goods` and `notes` are editorial. See docs/WORLD_DATA.md. Migration 20260818000058 (2026-08-26) rebalanced the roster to the owner's capital=10 / mid=4-8 / small=4 rule: 35 capital `goods` arrays gained deterministic filler entries (chosen by public.roster_rng, appended after the historically-researched entries) and 78 small-harbour arrays lost one entry each (the historically-researched entries otherwise stand). See that migration's header for the full account.

ports.name: Acapulco
ports.notes: American terminus of the Manila galleon from 1565; its annual fair traded Mexican silver for Asian goods.

ports.name: Accra
ports.notes: Three rival forts, Danish, Dutch and English, stood on this stretch of shore in the 17th century.

ports.name: Aden
ports.notes: Volcanic crater harbour holding the Red Sea gate; Albuquerque failed to take it in 1513, the Ottomans held it from 1538.

ports.name: Agadir
historicalNames: Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gué
ports.notes: Portuguese fort from 1505 until the Saadians stormed it in 1541, opening the Sous to their sugar trade.

ports.name: Alexandria
ports.notes: Mediterranean outlet of the Red Sea spice route until the Cape route drew the trade away after 1500.

ports.name: Algiers
ports.notes: Ottoman regency from 1516 and the leading Barbary corsair base in the western Mediterranean.

ports.name: Ambon
ports.notes: VOC headquarters in the Moluccas from 1605; site of the Amboyna executions of English merchants in 1623.

ports.name: Amsterdam
ports.notes: Seat of the VOC chamber and the 1602 stock exchange; the Wisselbank followed in 1609.

ports.name: Ancona
ports.notes: Papal free port on the Adriatic, linked by overland routes to Ragusa and the Ottoman Balkans.

ports.name: Angra
ports.notes: Terceira’s harbour, the obligatory rendezvous of the returning India and Indies fleets; its woad went north to the cloth towns.

ports.name: Antalya
ports.notes: Ottoman naval harbour on the Pamphylian coast and outlet for Taurus cedar and pine.

ports.name: Antwerp
ports.notes: Scheldt river port and Europe’s dominant commodity market until the 1585 Spanish siege and blockade.

ports.name: Arkhangelsk
ports.notes: Founded 1584 on the Dvina; Russia’s only sea outlet to the west, opened by Chancellor’s 1553 voyage.

ports.name: Ayutthaya
ports.localName: พระนครศรีอยุธยา
ports.notes: Chao Phraya river capital of Siam, reachable by seagoing ships and host to Portuguese, Dutch, Japanese and French quarters.

ports.name: Banda Aceh
ports.notes: Sultanate at Sumatra’s northern tip, at its height under Iskandar Muda, 1607-1636, and a rival to Portuguese Malacca.

ports.name: Banda Neira
ports.notes: The Banda islands were the world’s only source of nutmeg and mace; Coen’s conquest of 1621 destroyed their society.

ports.name: Bandar Abbas
ports.notes: Renamed by Shah Abbas after 1622 and made Persia’s Gulf outlet, with English and Dutch factories.

ports.name: Banten
ports.notes: West Java pepper sultanate where the first Dutch fleet arrived in 1596 and the English opened a factory in 1603.

ports.name: Barcelona
ports.notes: Catalan maritime capital whose medieval Consolat de Mar code shaped Mediterranean commercial law.

ports.name: Basra
ports.notes: Shatt al-Arab river port and the Ottoman head of navigation linking the Gulf to Baghdad and Aleppo.

ports.name: Beirut
ports.notes: Outlet for Mount Lebanon raw silk, promoted by the Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II in the early 1600s.

ports.name: Belem
historicalNames: Santa Maria de Belém do Grão-Pará
ports.notes: Founded 1616 at the Amazon mouth to shut French and Dutch traders out of the river.

ports.name: Bergen
ports.notes: Site of the Hanseatic Bryggen kontor, which controlled the northern stockfish trade until 1754.

ports.name: Bilbao
ports.notes: Outlet for Biscayan iron and Castilian wool; its Consulado governed trade with Flanders and England.

ports.name: Bordeaux
ports.notes: Garonne river port and the historic source of the claret shipped to England in bulk.

ports.name: Boston
ports.notes: Founded 1630 by the Massachusetts Bay Company; its cod and shipbuilding drove the early New England economy.

ports.name: Bridgetown
ports.notes: English settlement of 1628; Barbados turned to sugar in the 1640s and became the model plantation colony.

ports.name: Bristol
ports.notes: Avon river port; John Cabot sailed from here in 1497 and its ships worked the Newfoundland fishery.

ports.name: Bruges
ports.notes: Hanseatic kontor city whose Zwin channel silted up, shifting its trade to Antwerp by 1500.

ports.name: Buenos Aires
ports.notes: Refounded 1580 on the Rio de la Plata; a legal backwater that thrived on contraband silver from Potosi.

ports.name: Busan
ports.notes: Site of the Waegwan, the walled Japan House that was Joseon Korea’s only licensed trading post with Tsushima.

ports.name: Cadiz
ports.notes: Atlantic outport of Seville and assembly point for the treasure fleets; raided by Drake in 1587.

ports.name: Cagliari
ports.notes: Spanish-held capital of Sardinia; its lagoon salt pans and tuna fisheries provisioned half the western Mediterranean.

ports.name: Calabar
ports.notes: Cross river trading town of the Efik, reached by ocean shipping through the Calabar estuary.

ports.name: Calais
ports.notes: English-held wool staple town from 1347 until its recapture by France in 1558.

ports.name: Callao
ports.notes: Port of Lima from 1537 and the loading point of the Potosi silver bound north for the Panama fairs.

ports.name: Cape Coast
ports.notes: Fort begun by the Swedes in 1653 and English from 1664; later headquarters of the Gold Coast forts.

ports.name: Cape Town
ports.notes: Table Bay refreshment station founded by Jan van Riebeeck for the VOC in 1652.

ports.name: Cartagena
ports.notes: Founded 1533; the fortified treasure port of the Tierra Firme fleet, sacked by Drake in 1586.

ports.name: Cebu
ports.notes: Magellan was killed on nearby Mactan in 1521; Legazpi founded the first Spanish settlement here in 1565.

ports.name: Ceuta
ports.notes: Taken by Portugal in 1415, the first European foothold in North Africa; passed to Spain in 1668.

ports.name: Chennai
ports.notes: Fort St George was begun in 1640 on land granted to the English, the nucleus of Madras.

ports.name: Chios
ports.notes: Genoese Maona island until the Ottomans took it in 1566; the world’s only mastic groves, with silk and sweet wine beside them.

ports.name: Chittagong
ports.notes: The "Great Port of Bengal", held by Arakan with Portuguese freebooters until the Mughal conquest of 1666.

ports.name: Cidade Velha
ports.notes: Founded 1462 on Santiago, the first European city in the tropics and Portugal’s Cape Verde entrepot.

ports.name: Colombo
ports.notes: Portuguese fort from 1518 guarding the cinnamon lands; taken by the Dutch after a siege in 1656.

ports.name: Copenhagen
ports.notes: Danish capital commanding the Sound, where the Oresund toll was levied on all Baltic traffic from 1429.

ports.name: Corfu
ports.notes: Venetian fortress guarding the Adriatic entrance; withstood the Ottoman siege of 1537.

ports.name: Cork
ports.notes: Lee estuary harbour that provisioned Atlantic shipping with salt beef and butter.

ports.name: Cumana
ports.notes: Founded 1515 on the pearl coast opposite Cubagua, the earliest mainland Spanish town in South America.

ports.name: Dili
ports.notes: Portuguese Timor’s coast, worked for sandalwood from the 1510s; Dili became the capital in 1769.

ports.name: Diu
ports.notes: Portuguese fortress from 1535; the sea battle of Diu in 1509 broke the Mamluk-Gujarati fleet.

ports.name: Dublin
ports.notes: Viking-founded Liffey port and seat of English administration in Ireland.

ports.name: Dubrovnik
ports.notes: Ragusa, a tribute-paying republic under Ottoman protection whose neutral flag carried Balkan trade.

ports.name: Elmina
ports.notes: Sao Jorge da Mina, built 1482, was the first and richest European gold fort on the Guinea coast; Dutch-taken 1637.

ports.name: Famagusta
ports.notes: Venetian Cyprus’s fortified harbour, which fell after an eleven-month Ottoman siege in 1571.

ports.name: Feodosia
ports.notes: Caffa, the Genoese Crimean colony taken by the Ottomans in 1475 and thereafter their Black Sea seat.

ports.name: Fukuoka
ports.notes: Hakata was Japan’s oldest China-trade harbour and the landing point of the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281.

ports.name: Funchal
ports.notes: Madeiran capital settled from 1424; Europe’s first plantation sugar economy before Brazil eclipsed it.

ports.name: Fuzhou
ports.notes: Min river port designated by the Ming for tribute missions arriving from the Ryukyu kingdom.

ports.name: Galle
ports.notes: Southern Sri Lankan harbour taken by the Dutch in 1640 and rebuilt as their island stronghold.

ports.name: Gdansk
ports.notes: Vistula outlet through which Polish rye and naval stores fed the Dutch grain trade.

ports.name: Genoa
ports.notes: Republic whose Casa di San Giorgio financiers underwrote much of Habsburg Spain’s war debt.

ports.name: Gibraltar
ports.notes: Fortified rock commanding the strait between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean; Spanish-held until 1704.

ports.name: Goree
ports.notes: Island anchorage off Cape Verde peninsula, held in turn by Portugal, the Dutch from 1627 and France from 1677.

ports.name: Guangzhou
ports.notes: Pearl River city whose twice-yearly fairs were the licensed point of contact for foreign trade with China.

ports.name: Hadibu
ports.notes: Chief village of Socotra under the Mahra sultans; its aloes, dragon’s blood resin and ambergris drew Portuguese and Gujarati ships alike.

ports.name: Hagatna
ports.notes: Guam was the Manila galleon’s mid-Pacific watering stop; a Spanish mission was established in 1668.

ports.name: Hamburg
ports.notes: Elbe river port that absorbed much Antwerp trade after 1585; its Bank opened in 1619.

ports.name: Hanoi
ports.notes: Red River capital of Trinh-ruled Tonkin; Dutch and English factories traded here through the downstream port of Pho Hien.

ports.name: Havana
ports.notes: Assembly point where the New Spain and Tierra Firme fleets joined before the convoy run home to Seville.

ports.name: Heraklion
ports.notes: Candia, Venice’s Cretan capital, besieged by the Ottomans from 1648 and lost in 1669.

ports.name: Hirado
ports.notes: Held the Dutch factory from 1609 and the English from 1613, until both were moved or closed by 1641.

ports.name: Hoi An
ports.notes: Nguyen-ruled Cochinchina port with permanent Japanese and Chinese quarters, thriving on the shuinsen trade.

ports.name: Hong Kong
ports.notes: Its name derives from the incense trade of the harbour; a salt and fishing district until British occupation in 1841.

ports.name: Honolulu
ports.notes: Oahu harbour unknown to Europeans until Cook’s 1778 landfall; included as a Pacific waypoint, outside the 1500-1650 era.

ports.name: Hooghly
ports.notes: Portuguese river settlement of 1580 destroyed by the Mughals in 1632; the Dutch built Chinsurah beside it.

ports.name: Hoorn
ports.notes: Zuiderzee VOC chamber town; Cape Horn is named after it by Schouten and Le Maire in 1616.

ports.name: Hormuz
ports.notes: Island entrepot at the Gulf mouth, Portuguese from 1515 until an Anglo-Persian force took it in 1622.

ports.name: Incheon
ports.notes: Yellow Sea approach to Hanyang, the Joseon capital; the sea road for envoys and tribute to Ming China.

ports.name: Istanbul
ports.notes: Ottoman capital from 1453, straddling the Bosphorus between the Mediterranean and Black Sea trades.

ports.name: Izmir
ports.notes: Smyrna, which grew in the 17th century into the chief Levant Company outlet for Anatolian produce.

ports.name: Jaffna
ports.notes: Tamil kingdom conquered by Portugal in 1619; commanded the Palk Strait pearl and elephant trades.

ports.name: Jakarta
ports.notes: Jan Pieterszoon Coen razed Jayakarta in 1619 and built Batavia, the VOC capital in Asia.

ports.name: Jamestown
ports.notes: Established 1607 on the James river; the first English settlement in America to survive, on tobacco after 1614.

ports.name: Jeddah
ports.notes: Port of Mecca and the transhipment point where Indian goods met the pilgrim and Egyptian trades.

ports.name: Jeju
ports.notes: Former kingdom of Tamna, a royal horse-pasture island; Hendrick Hamel’s Dutch crew was wrecked here in 1653.

ports.name: Kagoshima
ports.notes: Satsuma’s castle port, where Francis Xavier landed in 1549 and from which Ryukyu was invaded in 1609.

ports.name: Kaliningrad
ports.notes: Founded 1255 as Konigsberg; ducal Prussian capital holding the Baltic amber monopoly.

ports.name: Kannur
ports.notes: Seat of the Kolathiri rajas; Portugal’s St Angelo fort of 1505 was one of its earliest in India.

ports.name: Karachi
ports.notes: Sindh coast anchorage near the site of the medieval Indus delta port of Debal.

ports.name: Khambhat
ports.notes: Gujarat’s great medieval emporium, whose gulf silted so badly that trade shifted to Surat by 1600.

ports.name: Kilwa
ports.notes: Swahili sultanate that controlled the Sofala gold trade before Portuguese sacking in 1505.

ports.name: Kingston upon Hull
ports.notes: Humber port handling English trade with the Baltic and, from the 1610s, Arctic whaling voyages.

ports.name: Kochi
ports.notes: Site of Fort Manuel, 1503, Portugal’s first Indian fort; the Dutch took the town in 1663.

ports.name: Kollam
ports.notes: Ancient Malabar pepper port with a Portuguese factory from 1503 and a Dutch one after 1661.

ports.name: Kozhikode
ports.notes: Vasco da Gama made landfall here in May 1498; the Zamorin’s city gave its name to calico cloth.

ports.name: Kupang
ports.notes: West Timor harbour where the VOC built Fort Concordia in 1653 to contest the sandalwood trade.

ports.name: La Rochelle
ports.notes: Huguenot merchant stronghold and the main French base for the Canadian fur trade until its 1628 siege.

ports.name: Lagos
ports.notes: Lagoon settlement named by Portuguese navigators in the late 15th century; a Benin outpost called Eko.

ports.name: Las Palmas
ports.notes: Founded 1478; standard first watering stop for Spanish fleets bound for the Americas.

ports.name: Le Havre
ports.notes: Founded by Francis I in 1517 as a purpose-built royal harbour at the Seine mouth.

ports.name: Leith
ports.notes: Port of Edinburgh and the hub of Scotland’s Baltic and Low Countries trade.

ports.name: Lisbon
ports.notes: Seat of the Casa da Índia; terminus of the Portuguese Carreira da Índia from 1501.

ports.name: Livorno
ports.notes: Made a free port by the Medici Livornine laws of 1591-1593, drawing foreign merchant colonies.

ports.name: London
ports.notes: Thames river port; the Royal Exchange opened 1571 and the English East India Company was chartered here in 1600.

ports.name: Longyearbyen
ports.notes: On Spitsbergen, sighted by Barentsz in 1596 and the base of Dutch and English whaling from 1611; the town itself dates from 1906.

ports.name: Luanda
historicalNames: São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda
ports.notes: Founded 1576 as Portugal’s Angolan capital; held by the Dutch from 1641 until Brazilian forces retook it in 1648.

ports.name: Lubeck
ports.notes: Leading city of the Hanseatic League and the seat of its diets on the Trave river.

ports.name: Macau
ports.notes: Portuguese settlement tolerated from 1557; the pivot of the Macau-Nagasaki silk-for-silver run.

ports.name: Machilipatnam
ports.notes: Golconda’s port, famous for kalamkari painted cottons and as the outlet for Deccan diamonds.

ports.name: Makassar
ports.notes: Gowa sultanate’s free port, where Portuguese, English and Danish traders evaded the Dutch spice monopoly until 1667.

ports.name: Malacca
ports.notes: Sultanate taken by Albuquerque in 1511; the strait chokepoint between the Indian Ocean and the China seas.

ports.name: Malaga
ports.notes: Chief Mediterranean outlet of Andalusia, exporting sweet wine and dried fruit across Europe.

ports.name: Malé
ports.notes: Seat of the Maldive sultans; cowrie shells by the shipload for Bengal and Guinea, coir rope, and the dried bonito every ocean crew carried.

ports.name: Malindi
ports.notes: Its sultan allied with Vasco da Gama in 1498 and provided the pilot who guided him to India.

ports.name: Manama
ports.notes: Bahrain, the centre of the Gulf pearl fishery, Portuguese-held 1521-1602 and then Safavid.

ports.name: Mangaluru
ports.notes: Kanara rice port that victualled Portuguese Goa; a Portuguese factory stood here from 1526.

ports.name: Manila
ports.notes: Spanish capital from 1571 and Asian terminus of the Acapulco galleon, exchanging American silver for Chinese silk.

ports.name: Marseille
ports.notes: France’s Mediterranean gateway and the base of its Levant trade under the Ottoman capitulations of 1536.

ports.name: Massawa
ports.notes: Red Sea gateway to the Ethiopian highlands, taken by the Ottomans in 1557.

ports.name: Matsumae
ports.notes: The Matsumae clan’s gate to Ezo: all Ainu trade — furs, salmon, deer hides, hawks — passed through this southernmost harbour of Hokkaido.

ports.name: Messina
ports.notes: Guards the strait between Sicily and Calabria; the Holy League fleet sailed from here to Lepanto in 1571.

ports.name: Middelburg
ports.notes: Zeeland capital, seat of the second-largest VOC chamber and a hub of the West India Company.

ports.name: Mocha
ports.notes: The world’s coffee port in the 17th century; European factories opened here from the 1610s.

ports.name: Mogadishu
ports.notes: Benadir coast city long famous for the woven cotton cloth Arab writers called "maqdishi".

ports.name: Mokpo
ports.notes: Southwestern harbour among the Jeolla islands; a Joseon garrison post guarding the grain-tribute sea route.

ports.name: Mombasa
ports.notes: Swahili city-state where Portugal built Fort Jesus in 1593 to command the coast.

ports.name: Island of Mozambique
ports.notes: Portuguese capital of East Africa and the standard wintering station on the Carreira da India.

ports.name: Mumbai
ports.notes: Seven islands ceded by Portugal to England in 1661 and leased to the East India Company in 1668.

ports.name: Muscat
ports.notes: Portuguese-held from 1507 until the Ya’ariba imams expelled them in 1650, launching Omani sea power.

ports.name: Myeik
ports.notes: Tenasserim port linked by a short overland portage to Ayutthaya, bypassing the Malacca Strait.

ports.name: Nagasaki
ports.notes: Opened to Portuguese ships in 1571; after 1641 the Dejima island factory was Japan’s only European window.

ports.name: Naha
ports.notes: Port of the Ryukyu kingdom, whose ships carried an entrepot trade between China, Japan and Southeast Asia.

ports.name: Nampo
ports.notes: Taedong river approach to Pyongyang, on the Yellow Sea route between Korea and Shandong.

ports.name: Nantes
ports.notes: Loire estuary port and the outlet for Bay of Bourgneuf salt and Breton linen.

ports.name: Naples
ports.notes: Capital of the Spanish viceroyalty and one of Europe’s largest cities in 1600.

ports.name: New York
ports.notes: New Amsterdam, chartered 1625 at the Hudson mouth as the Dutch West India Company’s beaver-trade capital.

ports.name: Ningbo
ports.notes: Ming-designated port for Japanese tribute missions and the base of the smuggling entrepot at Shuangyu, destroyed in 1548.

ports.name: Nuuk
ports.notes: Near the Norse Western Settlement abandoned in the 14th century; refounded as Godthaab in 1728.

ports.name: Old Goa
ports.notes: Taken by Albuquerque in 1510 and made the capital of the Estado da India, "Goa Dourada".

ports.name: Oran
ports.notes: Spanish presidio from 1509, holding a bridgehead on the Algerian coast for nearly two centuries.

ports.name: Osaka
ports.notes: Hideyoshi’s castle town of 1583, which became the rice market and "kitchen" of Tokugawa Japan.

ports.name: Ouidah
ports.notes: Port of the kingdom of Hueda on the Slave Coast, where several European nations kept trading lodges.

ports.name: Palermo
ports.notes: Sicilian capital and the shipping point for the island grain that fed much of the Mediterranean.

ports.name: Palma de Mallorca
ports.notes: Balearic base of the medieval Majorcan chart-making school that supplied portolan charts to Atlantic pilots.

ports.name: Panama City
historicalNames: Nuestra Señora de la Asunción de Panamá
ports.notes: Founded 1519 as the Pacific end of the isthmus crossing; Morgan destroyed the old city in 1671.

ports.name: Paramaribo
ports.notes: Suriname river settlement founded by the English in 1651 and ceded to the Dutch in 1667.

ports.name: Patras
ports.notes: Ottoman-held Gulf of Corinth port; English ships loaded currants here for the London market.

ports.name: Pattani
ports.notes: Malay sultanate on the Gulf of Siam where the Dutch opened their first Southeast Asian factory in 1602.

ports.name: Plymouth
ports.notes: Devon naval harbour; Drake’s circumnavigation began and ended here (1577-1580).

ports.name: Ponta Delgada
ports.notes: Azorean port where returning India and Indies fleets took on water and awaited naval escort.

ports.name: Port Louis
ports.notes: Uninhabited Mauritius drew the Dutch from 1598 for its ebony forests; they planted the first sugar cane in 1639, and the harbour town proper came later under the French.

ports.name: Port Royal
ports.notes: English base on Jamaica after the 1655 conquest; a buccaneer haven until the earthquake of 1692 sank most of it.

ports.name: Porto
ports.notes: Douro river port whose shipyards at Vila Nova de Gaia built vessels for the India voyages.

ports.name: Portobelo
ports.notes: Caribbean end of the isthmus mule road; its trade fairs handled the Peruvian silver from 1597.

ports.name: Portsmouth
ports.notes: Site of the first known dry dock in England, built for Henry VII in 1495.

ports.name: Pulicat
ports.notes: Site of Fort Geldria, 1610, the first Dutch fortified factory on the Coromandel coast.

ports.name: Quanzhou
ports.notes: The Zayton praised by Marco Polo; its harbour silted and Ming sea bans pushed trade to neighbouring ports.

ports.name: Quebec City
ports.notes: Champlain’s habitation of 1608 at the narrowing of the St Lawrence, the capital of New France.

ports.name: Recife
ports.notes: Reef-sheltered port of Pernambuco and capital of Dutch Brazil under Johan Maurits, 1637-1644.

ports.name: Reykjavik
ports.notes: Icelandic farm settlement under the Danish trade monopoly of 1602; chartered as a town in 1786.

ports.name: Rhodes
ports.notes: Base of the Knights Hospitaller until Suleiman took the fortress in 1522.

ports.name: Riga
ports.notes: Daugava river Hansestadt and the principal source of masts and cordage fibre for western navies.

ports.name: Rio de Janeiro
historicalNames: São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro
ports.notes: Founded 1565 in Guanabara Bay after the expulsion of the French colony of France Antarctique.

ports.name: Rotterdam
ports.notes: Maas river port and one of the six VOC chambers established in 1602.

ports.name: Safi
ports.notes: Portuguese-held 1508-1541; the Atlantic outlet for Marrakesh and its Sous sugar refineries.

ports.name: Saint-Louis
ports.notes: French post founded 1659 on an island in the Senegal river mouth, controlling the gum-arabic trade.

ports.name: Saint-Malo
ports.notes: Corsair port; Jacques Cartier sailed from here to the St Lawrence in 1534.

ports.name: Sakai
ports.notes: Self-governing merchant city and gun-founding centre, absorbed under Oda and Toyotomi rule after 1568.

ports.name: Sale
ports.notes: Bou Regreg corsair republic of the 1620s-1660s, manned partly by Moriscos expelled from Spain.

ports.name: Salvador
historicalNames: São Salvador da Bahia de Todos os Santos
ports.notes: Founded 1549 in the Bay of All Saints as the first capital of Brazil; briefly Dutch-held in 1624-1625.

ports.name: San Juan
ports.notes: Its El Morro castle, begun 1539, guarded the first Spanish landfall on the run in from the Atlantic.

ports.name: Sanlucar de Barrameda
ports.notes: Mouth of the Guadalquivir; Magellan sailed from here in 1519 and Elcano returned to it in 1522.

ports.name: Santa Cruz de Tenerife
ports.notes: Tenerife’s roadstead from the conquest of 1494; casks of Canary malmsey left here for London, Seville and the Indies.

ports.name: Santo Domingo
ports.notes: Founded 1496, the oldest continuously inhabited European city in the Americas and seat of the first audiencia.

ports.name: Santos
ports.notes: Founded 1546 on the estuary below the Serra do Mar; Cavendish raided it during his 1591 voyage.

ports.name: Sao Tome
ports.notes: Equatorial island settled from 1493; its sugar mills were the model later carried to Brazil.

ports.name: Setubal
ports.notes: Sado estuary salt pans supplied the salt that preserved northern European herring and cod catches.

ports.name: Seville
ports.notes: Guadalquivir river port holding the Crown monopoly on the Indies trade through the Casa de Contratacion, 1503-1717.

ports.name: Shimonoseki
ports.notes: Guards the Kanmon Strait between Honshu and Kyushu, the funnel for all Inland Sea coastal traffic.

ports.name: Sofala
ports.notes: Swahili gold port for the Zimbabwe plateau; Portugal built its fort here in 1505.

ports.name: Soyo
ports.notes: Mpinda at the Congo river mouth, the port of the kingdom of Kongo and Diogo Cao’s landfall in 1483.

ports.name: Split
ports.notes: Venetian-held Dalmatian town; its scala from 1592 funnelled Ottoman caravan goods to Venice.

ports.name: St. Augustine
ports.notes: Founded 1565 to guard the Bahama Channel where the treasure fleets turned north; oldest European city in the United States.

ports.name: St. George's
ports.notes: Settled after the Sea Venture wreck of 1609; a mid-Atlantic waypoint on the homeward sailing route from the Caribbean.

ports.name: St. John's
ports.notes: Sheltered harbour used by fishing fleets from the early 1500s; Gilbert claimed it for England in 1583.

ports.name: Stockholm
ports.notes: Swedish capital exporting Falun copper, which financed the crown through the Thirty Years War.

ports.name: Suakin
ports.notes: Coral-built Ottoman harbour and a principal embarkation point for pilgrims crossing to Jeddah.

ports.name: Suez
ports.notes: Head of the Red Sea and the Ottoman shipyard from which fleets sailed against the Portuguese in 1538.

ports.name: Surabaya
ports.notes: East Java river port and shipbuilding town, subdued by Sultan Agung of Mataram in 1625.

ports.name: Surat
ports.notes: Mughal India’s chief western port; the English factory of 1613 was their first foothold in India.

ports.name: Sydney
ports.notes: Port Jackson was settled in 1788; Dutch ships charted Australia’s west and north coasts from 1606, not this shore.

ports.name: Tainan
ports.notes: The VOC built Fort Zeelandia here in 1624; Zheng Chenggong expelled the Dutch in 1662.

ports.name: Tallinn
ports.notes: Reval, the Hanseatic outlet for Russian goods coming west from Novgorod.

ports.name: Tangier
ports.notes: Held by Portugal from 1471; passed to England in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza’s dowry.

ports.name: Ternate
ports.notes: Clove sultanate; the Portuguese fort of 1522 was expelled in 1575 and the Dutch took over from 1607.

ports.name: Thanlyin
ports.notes: Syriam, where the Portuguese adventurer Filipe de Brito ruled from 1600 until his execution in 1613.

ports.name: Thessaloniki
ports.notes: Ottoman Balkan port whose Sephardic community, settled after 1492, made it a woollen-cloth centre.

ports.name: Tidore
ports.notes: Ternate’s twin and rival clove sultanate; Spain garrisoned a fort here against the Dutch from 1606 to 1663.

ports.name: Tokyo
ports.notes: Edo, seat of the Tokugawa shogunate from 1603 and supplied by coastal shipping into Edo Bay.

ports.name: Tongyeong
ports.notes: Seat of the combined Three Provinces Naval Command from 1604, in the strait where the battle of Hansando was fought.

ports.name: Torshavn
ports.notes: Faroese Tinganes assembly site and the islands’ single licensed trading harbour under Danish rule.

ports.name: Toulon
ports.notes: French royal galley base on the Provencal coast from the early 16th century.

ports.name: Trabzon
ports.notes: Black Sea terminus of the Tabriz caravan road; the Byzantine successor empire here fell in 1461.

ports.name: Tripoli
ports.notes: Levant Company factory town and outlet for the caravan road running inland to Aleppo.

ports.name: Tripoli
ports.notes: Mediterranean terminus of the Fezzan caravan route; held by the Knights of Malta 1530-1551.

ports.name: Trondheim
ports.notes: Nidaros, medieval seat of the Norwegian archbishopric and outlet for Roros copper from 1644.

ports.name: Tsushima
ports.notes: The So clan’s island domain held the sole licence for Japan’s trade and diplomacy with Joseon Korea.

ports.name: Tunis
ports.notes: Hafsid then Ottoman capital whose harbour of La Goulette was taken by Charles V in 1535.

ports.name: Turku
ports.notes: Abo, the administrative and trading centre of Swedish Finland at the Aura river mouth.

ports.name: Ulsan
ports.notes: One of the three ports opened to Japanese traders in 1426; besieged during the Imjin War in 1597-98.

ports.name: Valencia
ports.notes: Silk-weaving city; its Llotja de la Seda commodity exchange was completed in 1548.

ports.name: Valletta
ports.notes: Founded 1566 by the Knights of St John after the Great Siege; corsairing base against Ottoman shipping.

ports.name: Valparaiso
ports.notes: Port of Santiago from 1544, sending Chilean wheat north to Peru; raided by Drake in 1578.

ports.name: Vardo
ports.notes: Norway’s northeasternmost fortress town, meeting point of Pomor traders and Arctic passage-seekers.

ports.name: Venice
ports.notes: Lagoon republic whose state Arsenal could fit out a galley in a day at its 16th-century peak.

ports.name: Veracruz
historicalNames: La Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz
ports.notes: New Spain’s Atlantic port, where Cortes landed in 1519 and the fortress of San Juan de Ulua sheltered the fleets.

ports.name: Visby
ports.notes: Gotland town whose sea law circulated across the Baltic; sacked by Denmark in 1361 and in decline thereafter.

ports.name: Willemstad
ports.notes: Dutch West India Company took Curacao in 1634 for its salt pans and its deep Schottegat harbour.

ports.name: Xiamen
ports.notes: Fujian island harbour and the base from which Zheng Chenggong ran his maritime empire in the 1650s.

ports.name: Yeosu
ports.notes: Headquarters of Yi Sun-sin’s Left Jeolla naval command, from which the turtle ships sailed in 1592.

ports.name: Zakynthos
ports.notes: Venetian island whose currant vineyards supplied the English trade — “Zante currants” still carry its name.

ports.name: Zanzibar
ports.notes: Swahili island town on the monsoon route; Omani control from 1698 made it the region’s chief entrepot.
